headline: High-risk shared-filesystem and MCP pathways make Continue’s default tool use dangerous alongside Airbyte’s broad egress.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read workspace files and use MCP, so attacker-controlled content in shared files or MCP outputs could influence its tool use. Airbyte has broad network egress and API access, but no documented direct ingestion path from Continue. The interaction exists via shared filesystem/manual handoff, not a proven default bridge.
conditions: IF Continue reads a file produced by Airbyte and treats it as instructions
IF an MCP server returns untrusted content that Continue forwards into tool calls
mitigations: Restrict shared folders to read-only for Continue
Disable MCP servers not needed for the task
Use a separate workspace for Airbyte outputs
Add a manual review step before any tool call
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between producer and consumer

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airbyte touches business data and has broad network egress; Continue reads workspace files and editor buffers and may send context to a chosen model provider. If both share a workspace, sensitive data can flow from Airbyte outputs into Continue prompts and then off-host. This is not proven by default, but the shared-filesystem path is explicit.
conditions: IF Airbyte writes business data into a workspace Continue can read
IF Continue sends that workspace content to a remote model provider
mitigations: Keep Airbyte outputs outside the IDE workspace
Use a local-only model provider in Continue
Redact sensitive fields before opening files in Continue
Separate credentials and data directories
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data loss prevention

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue has write_filesystem and shared state via filesystem across instances; Airbyte is a data-engineering system that can call APIs and emit files, so overlapping writes to the same workspace can race or overwrite artifacts. Airbyte itself does not request filesystem write in the profile, so the conflict is asymmetric, but the shared-state pathway is real.
conditions: IF Airbyte and Continue write to the same directory
IF multiple Continue instances operate on the same workspace without locking
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Turn on file locking in the orchestrator
Avoid concurrent edits during Airbyte runs
Use git branches per agent
requires-engineering: add coordination primitives around shared files

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can act on workspace content and tool outputs, while Airbyte can generate data artifacts and call APIs. If Continue treats Airbyte-produced files as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect code or downstream actions. There is no evidence of automatic action-taking by Airbyte, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Continue uses Airbyte output as source-of-truth without verification
IF a downstream workflow consumes Continue’s edited artifacts
mitigations: Require human review of Airbyte-derived files
Add checksum or schema validation before reuse
Keep generated artifacts in a staging folder
Limit Continue to suggestion-only mode
requires-engineering: add explicit verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: Airbyte touches business data and Continue handles source code, open buffers, and model-provider API keys. If business data includes regulated records and Continue sends context to a third-party model provider, retention or residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated business data is opened in Continue
IF the selected model provider retains prompts beyond policy
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the IDE workspace
Use a provider with an acceptable DPA
Disable prompt logging where possible
Review retention settings before use
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing by data class
